# Basin-scale flood routing — the upstream-flood signal

Closes the river-routing blind spot documented twice on this research branch
(`BACKTEST.md` "river-routing blind spot"; `LIMPOPO_CASE_STUDY.md` verdict): the frozen
per-cell detector reads local rain-on-saturated-soil, so a downstream cell inheriting a
flood wave from upstream rain is warned late or not at all — Chokwe was silent until
in-event in Feb 1977 while the upstream escarpment cell had warned 128 h earlier, and the
flood rule proper missed the first Feb-2000 river rise at every lower-basin point. The
classic South African case is the same shape: Laingsburg, 25 Jan 1981 — the Buffels River
flood wave came down from catchment rain upstream of the town.

**The fix is a NEW ADDITIVE signal, not a re-tune.** The tuned detector config
(`detector/detector_config_tuned.json`, sha-frozen) and the 2018+ holdout are untouched.
Basin thresholds were chosen on pre-2018 history only (section 4); the Dec 2025 – Feb 2026
Limpopo event is run as a blind demonstration with the already-frozen numbers (section 5).

## 1. Terrain / basin dataset

**Chosen: HydroBASINS v1c, level 7, Africa** (standard attribute set), from the HydroSHEDS
project (WWF).

* **Why**: it directly provides what routing needs — sub-basin polygons with river-network
  topology (`NEXT_DOWN` chains), along-network distance to the basin sink (`DIST_MAIN`, km),
  and areas (`SUB_AREA`, `UP_AREA`) — no DEM processing, no home-grown flow direction. At
  0.25° a level-7 sub-basin (typically 2,000–8,000 km²) is a few ERA5 cells: the right
  granularity. Alternatives evaluated: Copernicus DEM GLO-90 (reachable on AWS open data,
  license fine, but would require deriving D8 flow directions from elevation — strictly
  worse hydrology than an authoritative river network for more work); ETOPO 2022 / GMTED2010
  (hosts unreachable from the build environment, same DEM objection).
* **License**: the HydroSHEDS version-1 license (Technical Documentation, Appendix A) —
  freely available for scientific, educational **and commercial** use; **attribution
  required** ([hydrosheds.org/products/hydrobasins](https://www.hydrosheds.org/products/hydrobasins)).
  Citation: *Lehner, B., Grill G. (2013): Global river hydrography and network routing:
  baseline data and new approaches to study the world's large river systems. Hydrological
  Processes, 27(15): 2171–2186.* The attribution block is embedded in the committed
  artifact (`basin_map.json` → `source`) so it travels with the data.
* **Access note (honest)**: `data.hydrosheds.org` and the GEE catalog are blocked by this
  build environment's egress proxy. The build used a faithful public GitHub mirror of the
  HydroBASINS shapefile→GeoJSON conversion
  ([github.com/SilliamBims/WikiGroundWatersheds](https://github.com/SilliamBims/WikiGroundWatersheds),
  attribution preserved, full standard attribute set verified present). The regeneration
  script accepts the canonical shapefile as first-choice input (`--shapefile`) and the
  mirror as fallback (`--geojson-dir`); build-time sanity assertions pin the load-bearing
  topology facts either way.

### The committed artifact

`weather/frappe/src/control/warnings_engine/basin_map.json` — **336 KB minified JSON**,
regenerated by `build_basin_map.py`:

* region: lat −36…−10, lon 10…42 (Limpopo, Orange/Vaal, lower Zambezi/Okavango, Save,
  Incomati, Cape rivers, coastal basins);
* **8,324 ERA5 0.25° cells → containing level-7 sub-basin** (cell-center point-in-polygon;
  275 coastal cells snapped to the nearest polygon within 0.2° — an ERA5 coastal cell is
  part ocean while still covering river-mouth land, e.g. the Xai-Xai cell);
* **2,627 sub-basins → topology row** `[next_down, main_bas, dist_main_km, sub_area_km2,
  up_area_km2, rep_lat_idx, rep_lon_idx]`, where the rep cell (nearest the polygon
  centroid) is where the engine samples that sub-basin's rain.

Build-time sanity (asserted, not assumed): the six Limpopo case-study cells share one
`MAIN_BAS`; musina/thohoyandou/pafuri are upstream of chokwe with musina farthest
(+594 km along the network); all five are upstream of the xai_xai mouth cell. One honest
resolution artifact: the **mapai** 0.25° cell center falls in the **Changane** tributary
catchment, which joins the Limpopo *below* Chokwe — so mapai is upstream of xai_xai but
not of chokwe. That is correct hydrology for that cell's area, not a bug.

## 2. Signal design (engine module `basin.py`)

For a watch cell: walk the `NEXT_DOWN`-reversed graph to get all strictly-upstream
sub-basins within 1,500 km of network distance (the cell's own sub-basin excluded — local
rain is the frozen detector's job); sample up to 12 of them (largest area first within
distance bands 0–150 / 150–400 / 400–800 / 800–1,500 km, merged per rep cell); fetch
each sample cell's trailing 168 h of ERA5 precipitation; compute **area-weighted upstream
basin rain** over 72 h and 168 h. Fail-closed gates: no artifact, unmapped cell, upstream
area < 2,000 km², or less than half the sampled area having data ⇒ no signal.

Tiers (mm of area-weighted upstream rain; `severe_weather_basin_*` site-config overridable):

| tier | rule |
|---|---|
| advisory | 72 h ≥ 40, OR (168 h ≥ 100 AND 72 h ≥ 30) — the long-rain arm |
| heads_up | 72 h ≥ 70 |
| warning | 72 h ≥ 110 (pure burst, small catchments), OR **72 h ≥ 60 AND 168 h ≥ 120** (compound arm) |

Lag estimate (admin telemetry + record validity): rain-weighted mean flow distance ÷
4 km/h flood-wave celerity (Limpopo 2000: ~400 km in ~4 days). Record `valid_until` =
data horizon + clamp(lag + 24 h, 24 h, 120 h).

Surface: a distinct `upstream_flood` event class — its own calm copy in the message layer
(explicitly saying levels can rise "even if it stays dry where you are"; no "warning"
wording, no official taxonomy — test-enforced), its own record lifecycle, pushed only at
heads_up/warning via the existing severity-ranked push path. Admin precursors JSON carries
the full technical detail: sampled upstream cells, per-cell accumulations, flow distances,
weights, lag estimate, upstream area. Excluded by design from the propagation pass
(fail-closed class gate — a derived signal must not seed advisories or consensus) and from
the outcome ledger (`VERIFIABLE_CLASSES` — local-cell extremes cannot verify a river-routed
episode; river-gauge-based verification is a follow-up).

## 3. Validation protocol

`validate_basin.py` loads the **engine module itself** by file path (no copy of the math)
and replays it causally, hour by hour, over ERA5 hourly precipitation
(`s3://openmeteo`, anonymous, via `extraction/era5_extract.py`; CC-BY-4.0, "Weather data by
Open-Meteo.com"). Event dates were re-verified against public sources before scoring
(Laingsburg: SA History Online and 1981 flood literature — catchment rain 24–25 Jan 1981,
river through town midday 25 Jan; Limpopo 2000: FloodList/DFO — overflow at Chokwe/Xai-Xai
11–13 Feb, peak flow at Chokwe 13 Feb; 1977 and 2013 milestones as referenced in
`LIMPOPO_CASE_STUDY.md` §1). Threshold selection used **only** these pre-2018 cases plus
the 1995–2017 baseline below; nothing after 2017 informed any number.

## 4. Results — pre-2018 validation cases

Leads are against the documented downstream milestone; `local72` = the *target* cell's own
trailing 72 h rain when the tier first fired (the "no rain here yet" honesty check).
Verbatim harness output is in `basin_validation.json`.

### Feb 1977 — the original blind spot: CLOSED

| target | tier | first fired | lead | upstream 72 h | local 72 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chokwe | advisory | 31 Jan 14:00Z | **+11.4 d** | 40 mm | 41 mm |
| chokwe | heads_up | 7 Feb 23:00Z | **+4.0 d** | 71 mm | 59 mm |
| chokwe | warning | 9 Feb 02:00Z | **+2.9 d** | 86 mm | 95 mm |
| xai_xai | heads_up | 7 Feb 07:00Z | **+4.7 d** | 72 mm | 43 mm |
| xai_xai | warning | 8 Feb 10:00Z | **+3.6 d** | 98 mm | 68 mm |

The frozen detector's flood rule was **silent at Chokwe until 15 Feb (in-event)**; this
signal has a warning active 2.9 days before the 12 Feb inundation.

### Feb 2000 — warning with 3 mm of local rain

| target | tier | first fired | lead | upstream 72 h | local 72 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chokwe | advisory | 3 Jan 07:00Z | +38.7 d | 42 mm | 37 mm |
| chokwe | heads_up | 17 Jan 13:00Z | +24.5 d | 71 mm | 37 mm |
| chokwe | warning | 10 Feb 03:00Z | **+21 h** (vs 11 Feb overflow; ~3 d vs the 13 Feb Chokwe peak flow) | 71 mm | **3 mm** |
| xai_xai | advisory | 3 Jan 07:00Z | +38.7 d | 42 mm | 36 mm |
| xai_xai | heads_up / warning | — | **never fired** | — | — |

The January leads are real but belong to the *documented antecedent flood phase* (heavy
rain through Jan 2000), not clairvoyance about February. The February warning at Chokwe is
the signal working exactly as designed: 71 mm of basin-mean upstream rain while the Chokwe
cell itself had **3 mm** in 72 h. **Honest miss: Xai-Xai never reached heads_up** — its
larger catchment (410k km² incl. the drier Changane) dilutes the area-weighted mean below
the 70 mm bar; it got advisory only.

### Jan 2013

| target | tier | first fired | lead | upstream 72 h | local 72 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chokwe | advisory | 15 Jan 23:00Z | +6.0 d | 41 mm | 60 mm |
| chokwe | warning | 20 Jan 14:00Z | **+34 h** (vs 22 Jan evacuation) | 61 mm | 16 mm |
| xai_xai | advisory | 12 Jan 16:00Z | +9.3 d | 40 mm | 64 mm |
| xai_xai | warning | 21 Jan 01:00Z | **+23 h** | 62 mm | 26 mm |

(The frozen detector's own flood-severe at Chokwe came 21 Jan 10:00 with 14 h lead —
below the class's 24 h minimum, scored a miss. The basin warning beats it by ~20 h and the
advisory by 5 days.)

### Laingsburg, 25 Jan 1981 — documented LIMIT case, effectively a miss

| target | tier | first fired | lead | upstream 72 h | local 72 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| laingsburg | advisory | 25 Jan 04:00Z | **+2 h** (vs ~06:00Z river overflow) | 40 mm | 46 mm |
| laingsburg | heads_up | 25 Jan 13:00Z | −7 h (in-event; town flooded ~12:00Z) | 74 mm | 72 mm |
| laingsburg | warning | — | never | — | — |

Honest verdict: **basin routing adds almost nothing at Laingsburg scale.** The mapped
Buffels catchment above the town is 2,264 km² (~4 ERA5 cells) and the rain-to-flood time
was hours; ERA5 also smears the storm across the town's own cell (local 72 h ≈ upstream
72 h). A 2 h advisory lead is real but operationally thin. Events this small and fast are
the *flash-flood detector's* job; the basin signal's value begins at sub-basin scales of
tens of thousands of km² where the routing lag is days. This limit is by construction
(0.25° cells + level-7 sub-basins), not fixable by tuning, and is stated here rather than
hidden.

### 1995–2017 baseline at Chokwe — the false-alarm denominator

Causal replay of all 23 pre-2018 years (201k hours; vectorized fast path asserted
equivalent to the engine math on 200 random samples per run):

| tier | episodes | per year | episode dates |
|---|---|---|---|
| warning | 4 | **0.17/yr** | 14 Feb 1996 (×2, one event), 10 Feb 2000, 20 Jan 2013 |
| heads_up | 7 | **0.30/yr** | Jan+Feb 1996, Jan 2000, Feb 2000, Jan 2013 |
| advisory | 53 | 2.30/yr | wet-season clusters |

**Every warning and every heads_up episode in 23 years falls inside a documented Limpopo
flood period** (Jan–Feb 1996: the river's documented return to overflow; 2000; 2013).
The compound warning arm (72 h ≥ 60 AND 168 h ≥ 120) was chosen *because* those are the
only three periods in the baseline that reach it — that is threshold selection on pre-2018
data, stated plainly. The advisory tier at 2.3/yr is a muted "worth knowing" surface and
is the deliberate price of the 11-day early notices above.

## 5. Blind demonstration — Dec 2025 – Feb 2026 (no tuning input)

Run with the exact thresholds frozen after section 4. Milestone: the 20 Jan 2026 Xai-Xai
area evacuation order (~115,000 people; national disaster declared 18 Jan).

| target | tier | first fired | lead vs 20 Jan | upstream 72 h | local 72 h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chokwe | advisory | 22 Dec 10:00Z | +28.6 d | 40 mm | 16 mm |
| chokwe | heads_up | 12 Jan 03:00Z | +7.9 d | 73 mm | 228 mm |
| chokwe | warning | 12 Jan 15:00Z | **+7.4 d** | 111 mm | 214 mm |
| xai_xai | heads_up | 10 Jan 14:00Z | +9.4 d | 72 mm | 82 mm |
| xai_xai | warning | 11 Jan 08:00Z | **+8.7 d** | 110 mm | 113 mm |

The 22 Dec advisory also precedes the documented first flooding phase (~25 Dec,
Waterberg/Capricorn) by ~3 days. Caveat stated honestly: in 2026, unlike 1977/2000, the
lower-basin cells were themselves drenched (local 72 h > 80 mm), so the frozen detector
also fired here (see the case study) — the basin signal's *unique* value in this event is
the tier-graded upstream quantity and the ~9-day warning-tier lead at the mouth, not
rescuing a silent cell.

| event | best basin lead (warning tier) | local rain at first warning | frozen detector at same target |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1977 Chokwe | +2.9 d | 95 mm (rising) | silent until in-event (+3 d late) |
| 1977 Xai-Xai | +3.6 d | 68 mm | in-event only |
| 2000 Chokwe | +21 h (+3 d vs peak flow) | **3 mm** | flood rule missed the first rise |
| 2000 Xai-Xai | **miss** (advisory only) | — | flash-flood rule only |
| 2013 Chokwe | +34 h | 16 mm | 14 h (below 24 h minimum) |
| 1981 Laingsburg | **miss** (2 h advisory) | 46 mm | (flash-flood territory) |
| 2026 blind demo | +7.4…+8.7 d | heavy | also fired (see case study) |

## 7. Known limits and follow-ups

1. **Small, fast catchments** (Laingsburg): below ~10k km² and ~24 h routing lag the
   signal degenerates toward local detection. Do not expect value there.
2. **Basin-size dilution**: one fixed mm-threshold set across a 340k km² catchment mean is
   coarse — Xai-Xai 2000 shows the cost. A per-cell climatological normalization of the
   upstream quantity (percentile against that catchment's own history, reusing the
   climatology machinery) is the natural v2.
3. **Observed rain only**: upstream *forecast* aggregation (the fusion module's forecast
   covers only the local cell) would add ~1–3 days of lead. Documented follow-up.
4. **No river-gauge verification**: the outcome ledger excludes `upstream_flood`; wiring
   GRDC/DWS gauge data would make episodes verifiable.
5. **Celerity is a constant** 4 km/h; real wave speed varies with channel and flood size.
   Only the lag estimate / validity window depends on it, not the tiers.
6. **ERA5 lag**: like every observed-data signal in this engine, availability lags
   real time ~2–7 days on the S3 archive; the multi-day leads above are leads over the
   *data horizon* the engine actually has. Config-switching to the API source removes most
   of that lag.

## Files

* `build_basin_map.py` — regenerates `basin_map.json` (canonical shapefile or mirror input;
  sanity-asserted).
* `validate_basin.py` — causal replay of the engine math over the historical cases +
  baseline; writes `basin_validation.json`.
* `basin_validation.json` — verbatim results consumed by the tables above.
* Engine: `weather/frappe/src/control/warnings_engine/basin.py` (+ `basin_map.json`),
  copy in `weather/frappe/src/warnings_engine/messages.py`, tests in
  `weather/frappe/tests/test_sw5_basin.py`.

Extracted ERA5 series and the read cache stay uncommitted (same policy as all extraction
work). Attribution carried at runtime: "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com" (CC-BY-4.0) on
every serving surface, HydroSHEDS attribution embedded in the artifact.
